paragraphs.heading: When forces cancel
paragraphs.text: In classical mechanics, a particle is in mechanical equilibrium when the net force on it is zero. A system made of many parts is in equilibrium when the net force on every one of those parts is zero. The same idea can be put in other, equivalent ways: the momentum of each part stays constant, or the velocity stays constant. For turning motion, equilibrium means the net torque is zero and angular momentum is conserved.

paragraphs.heading: Still or steady
paragraphs.text: If a particle in equilibrium has zero velocity, it is in static equilibrium. A paperweight on a desk is one example, and so is a Jenga stack that is not in the middle of collapsing. Moving things can be in equilibrium too: a child sliding down a slide at constant speed is in mechanical equilibrium, but not static equilibrium, as seen from the slide or the earth. Since every particle in equilibrium has constant velocity, you can always find an inertial reference frame in which it is standing still.

paragraphs.heading: Stable or unstable
paragraphs.text: An important property of any equilibrium is its stability. When the potential energy is at a local maximum, the equilibrium is unstable: move the system even a tiny distance and the forces push it farther away. When the potential energy is at a local minimum, a small nudge brings forces that tend to restore the balance. If a system has more than one stable state, any of them with potential energy above the absolute lowest is called metastable.

paragraphs.heading: Neutral states and saddles
paragraphs.text: In a truly neutral state the energy does not change, and the equilibrium covers a finite width. This is sometimes called marginally stable, or a state of indifference. In more than one dimension, a system can be stable when pushed along x but unstable when pushed along y, a case known as a saddle point. In general, an equilibrium is only called stable if it is stable in every direction.

paragraphs.heading: A hand on a spring
paragraphs.text: Picture a person pressing a spring to a chosen point and holding it there. At that point the push and the spring's reaction are equal, so the system is in mechanical equilibrium. When the push is taken away, the spring goes back to its original state.

paragraphs.heading: When the sums fall short
paragraphs.text: Sometimes the equilibrium equations, which balance forces and moments, are not enough to work out all the forces and reactions. Such a case is called statically indeterminate. These problems can often be solved with information from outside the standard equilibrium equations.

paragraphs.heading: The gömböc
paragraphs.text: A question of special interest is how few static equilibria a uniform, convex body can have when it rests under gravity on a flat surface. For flat, two-dimensional shapes the smallest number is 4. In three dimensions, though, an object can be built with just one stable and one unstable balance point. Such an object is called a gömböc.
